questions.text: Under the 2024 IRR (Trap #49), what percentage of seats in an assembly hall must be designated as wheelchair spaces, and what replaced the old tiered table?

options.text: 2% of total seating capacity under the 2024 IRR, replacing the old 4-per-300-seat tiered table, ensuring greater accessibility
3% of total seating capacity under the 2024 IRR, replacing the old tiered table (4–50 seats → 2 spaces, etc.)
5% of total seating capacity under the 2024 IRR, a single flat rate for all assembly occupancies, simplifying compliance
4% of total seating capacity under the 2024 IRR, replacing the old variable-percentage formula, providing a more uniform standard

rationale.summary: Trap #49: 2024 IRR replaces the old tiered table with a flat 3% of total seating capacity for wheelchair spaces.
rationale.explanation: Trap #49 in the article. The old BP 344 IRR used a tiered table: 4–50 seats → 2 wheelchair spaces; 51–300 → 4 spaces; 301–500 → 6 spaces; 500+ → additional 1 per 100. The 2024 IRR replaced this with a single flat rule: 3% of total seating capacity shall be wheelchair spaces (Sec. 4 App. D). Additionally, 5% of general waiting area seating must be designated priority seats for PWDs — a separate provision. The exam tests whether candidates know the new flat rate versus the old tiered table.
common_misconceptions: Using the old tiered table for a 2024 IRR question — the flat 3% rule replaced all tiered formulas
Confusing the 3% wheelchair space quota with the 5% priority seating quota — these are two distinct requirements

questions.explanation: 2024 IRR: 3% flat rate for wheelchair spaces in assembly (plus 5% priority seating) — the old tiered table is superseded.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR Sec. 4 App. D; Trap #49

questions.text: What is the maximum ramp run between landings under BP 344 Philippine standard, and how does this differ from the U.S. ADA figure that is commonly misapplied?

options.text: Philippines: 9000 mm maximum; U.S. ADA: 10500 mm — the Philippine standard is more restrictive
Philippines: 10500 mm maximum; U.S. ADA: 9000 mm — the Philippine standard allows longer runs
Philippines: 7500 mm maximum; U.S. ADA: 9000 mm — both standards require landings more frequently than most reviewers teach
Philippines: 10500 mm maximum; U.S. ADA: 10500 mm — both standards use the same maximum ramp run length

rationale.summary: Trap #2: Philippines (BP 344) allows 10500 mm maximum ramp run; U.S. ADA uses 9000 mm.
rationale.explanation: Trap #2 in the article. Philippine BP 344 IRR specifies a maximum ramp run of 10,500 mm (10.5 m) before a rest landing is required. U.S. ADA specifies 9,000 mm (9 m). Philippine reviewers often incorrectly cite the ADA figure of 9 m. The Philippine standard actually allows longer runs than ADA. This is counterintuitive — many assume the Philippine standard would be equal or more restrictive, but the 10.5 m figure is the correct Philippine value.
common_misconceptions: Using the ADA's 9000 mm figure as the Philippine standard — BP 344 specifies the longer 10500 mm
Assuming Philippine standards are always more restrictive than ADA — the ramp run maximum is actually more permissive

questions.explanation: Philippines: 10500 mm max ramp run (not the ADA's 9000 mm) — a frequently misapplied foreign standard.

questions.text: An exam question asks for the minimum ramp landing length under BP 344. A student answers 1500 mm because that is the stair landing and approach clear floor dimension. According to Trap #3, is the student correct?

options.text: Yes — 1500 mm is the correct ramp landing length, consistent across both ramp landings and stair landings
No — ramp landings are 1800 mm; 1500 mm applies to stair landings and approach clear floor areas, not ramp landings
No — ramp landings must be 2000 mm to provide enough space for a wheelchair to fully clear the slope
Yes — 1500 mm applies to both ramp and stair landings since BP 344 uses a single landing standard

questions.rationale: Trap #3: ramp landings = 1800 mm; stair landings and approach clear floors = 1500 mm. These are different. Trap #3 in the article. BP 344 specifies ramp landings (at top, bottom, and intermediate points) at 1800 mm in length. Stair landings and approach clear floor areas use 1500 mm. The ALE frequently places both dimensions in the same question to exploit this confusion. The mnemonic from the article's summary table: 'Ramp landing vs. stair landing → Ramp = 1800 mm; Stair = 1500 mm.' The student's answer of 1500 mm is the wrong dimension applied to the wrong element.
questions.explanation: Classic pair: ramp landing = 1800 mm; stair landing / approach clear floor = 1500 mm. Never swap these.

questions.text: According to Trap #12 in the Top 50 Traps article, what is the maximum riser height for accessible stairs under BP 344, and how does this differ from the PD 1096 general stair maximum?

options.text: BP 344 accessible stairs: 175 mm maximum riser; PD 1096 general stairs: 200 mm maximum
BP 344 accessible stairs: 150 mm maximum riser; PD 1096 general stairs: 200 mm maximum
BP 344 accessible stairs: 150 mm maximum riser; PD 1096 general stairs: 180 mm maximum
BP 344 accessible stairs: 200 mm maximum riser; PD 1096 general stairs: 250 mm maximum

rationale.summary: Trap #12: BP 344 accessible stairs cap riser at 150 mm; PD 1096 general stairs allow up to 200 mm.
rationale.explanation: Trap #12 in the article. PD 1096 allows risers up to 200 mm for general occupancy stairs. BP 344 is more restrictive for accessible stairs, capping risers at 150 mm. The lower riser height reduces the step height demand on persons with mobility impairments, reducing the energy and muscle force required per step. On the ALE, whenever the question specifies 'accessible staircase,' the BP 344 maximum of 150 mm is the correct answer — not the PD 1096 value of 200 mm.
common_misconceptions: Applying PD 1096's 200 mm maximum to accessible stairs — BP 344 is more restrictive at 150 mm
Selecting 175 mm as a middle ground — there is no middle value; the two standards are 150 mm (BP 344) and 200 mm (PD 1096)

questions.explanation: Accessible stair riser: 150 mm max (BP 344); general stair riser: 200 mm max (PD 1096) — BP 344 is always more restrictive.

questions.text: According to Trap #21, where does a wheelchair user make their turning maneuver when using an accessible elevator — inside the car or in the lobby?

options.text: Inside the car — the 1200 × 1400 mm car provides sufficient space for a standard wheelchair turning radius
In the elevator lobby — the 1800 × 1800 mm lobby provides the turning space the small car cannot
Inside the car for standard wheelchairs; in the lobby only for power wheelchairs and scooters
Either location is acceptable as long as the combined car-plus-lobby area equals 1800 × 1800 mm

rationale.summary: Trap #21: the wheelchair turn happens in the lobby (1800 × 1800 mm), not inside the car.
rationale.explanation: Trap #21 in the article. The standard accessible elevator car is 1200 mm wide × 1400 mm deep — not large enough for a wheelchair to make a full 180° turning maneuver (which requires ~1800 mm diameter). BP 344 requires the elevator lobby to provide 1800 × 1800 mm clear turning space. The user approaches in the lobby, turns if needed, then enters the car forward or backs in. The lobby, not the car, is the functional turning zone.
common_misconceptions: Believing the car is large enough for turning — 1200 × 1400 mm is too small for the 1800 mm turning circle
Treating 'inside the car' as correct because it feels intuitive — the lobby provides the mandatory turning space

questions.explanation: Turning happens in the lobby (1800 × 1800 mm) — the car (1200 × 1400 mm) is too small for a turning maneuver.

questions.text: Trap #29 identifies a counterintuitive emergency call button placement rule. At what height must the emergency call button in an accessible toilet be mounted, and why does it deviate from the standard operable controls range?

options.text: 900–1200 mm AFF — the same as all operable controls, to maintain design consistency
400–600 mm AFF — reachable from the floor by a fallen user who cannot stand or reach higher
300 mm AFF — at the base of the wall so it is always visible and reachable when crawling
700–800 mm AFF — consistent with the lower accessible handrail height and seated reach range

rationale.summary: Trap #29: emergency button at 400–600 mm AFF — reachable from the floor by a fallen user.
rationale.explanation: Trap #29 in the article. The standard operable controls range is 900–1200 mm AFF, but the emergency call button in an accessible toilet deliberately violates this range. The button must be at 400–600 mm AFF because it must be reachable by a user who has fallen to the floor and cannot stand or reach upward. A button at 900–1200 mm is unreachable by a prone or severely incapacitated user. This is one of the most counterintuitive specifications in BP 344 — the one control that is intentionally placed lower than the standard reach range.
common_misconceptions: Applying the standard 900–1200 mm operable range to the emergency button — this button is the explicit exception
Selecting 300 mm as 'even lower therefore better' — 400–600 mm is the specified range, not lower

questions.explanation: Emergency toilet button: 400–600 mm AFF — the one control intentionally below the standard 900–1200 mm reach range.

questions.text: Trap #38 addresses contrast percentage requirements in BP 344 for two different elements: tactile strips and stair nosings. What are the correct percentages for each?

options.text: Tactile strips: 30% luminance contrast; stair nosings: 50% luminance contrast
Tactile strips: 50% luminance contrast; stair nosings: 30% luminance contrast
Tactile strips: 50% luminance contrast; stair nosings: 50% luminance contrast — same requirement for both
Tactile strips: 70% luminance contrast; stair nosings: 30% luminance contrast — tactile strips require higher contrast

rationale.summary: Trap #38: tactile strips = 50% luminance contrast; stair nosings = 30% luminance contrast.
rationale.explanation: Trap #38 in the article. BP 344 specifies two different luminance contrast percentages for two different elements: tactile floor/wall surfaces require 50% luminance contrast with adjacent surfaces; stair nosings require only 30% luminance contrast. The trap is easy to construct on an exam by swapping the two percentages. Tactile strips need higher contrast because they must be visible from a standing or walking approach; stair nosings are already at foot level and require only moderate contrast.
common_misconceptions: Applying the same percentage to both elements — they have different contrast requirements (50% vs. 30%)
Selecting 70% for tactile strips as 'even safer' — 50% is the specified standard, not 70%

questions.explanation: Two contrast standards: tactile strips = 50%; stair nosings = 30%. A common exam trap swaps these two values.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 IRR App. B / Stairs section; Trap #38

questions.text: Trap #46 addresses vertical clearance for accessible parking. What minimum vertical clearance must accessible parking spaces provide, and why does this differ from standard parking clearance?

options.text: 2100 mm minimum — the same as standard parking, since accessible spaces do not require additional clearance
2200 mm minimum — 100 mm more than standard parking, to allow a person standing beside the car to open the door fully
2300 mm minimum — required exclusively for accessible spaces to accommodate raised-roof vans
2500 mm minimum — providing generous clearance for all vehicle types used by PWDs, including high-roof vans

questions.rationale: Trap #46: accessible parking requires 2300 mm minimum vertical clearance — exclusively for raised-roof vans. Trap #46 in the article. Standard parking structures typically provide 2100–2200 mm vertical clearance. BP 344 IRR requires a minimum of 2300 mm vertical clearance specifically at accessible parking spaces to accommodate raised-roof vans (wheelchair-accessible vehicles with elevated rooflines). This is not required throughout the entire parking structure — only at the accessible spaces. An accessible parking level at 2100 mm standard clearance would physically prevent raised-roof van access to the only spaces intended for the users who need them most.
questions.explanation: Accessible parking: 2300 mm min vertical clearance (vs. standard 2100 mm) — raised-roof vans require the additional headroom.

questions.text: A review question asks for the 'standard' ramp slope for accessible ramps in the Philippines. An examinee answers 1:12. According to the Top 50 Traps article, is this answer correct?

options.text: Yes — 1:12 is the Philippine standard ramp slope, matching both the ADA and BP 344 requirements
No — 1:12 is the maximum allowed slope; 1:20 is the preferred standard and 1:15 is acceptable under BP 344
No — 1:12 is too steep; the only compliant ramp slope is 1:20 with no exceptions under the 2024 IRR
Yes — 1:12 is correct for renovations; 1:15 applies only to new construction projects

rationale.summary: Trap #1: 1:12 is the MAXIMUM, not the standard. BP 344 prefers 1:20 and accepts 1:15.
rationale.explanation: This is Trap #1 in the Top 50 Traps article. BP 344 2024 IRR specifies: 1:20 is the preferred/ideal slope; 1:15 is acceptable; 1:12 is the maximum allowed (only where space constraints make gentler slopes impossible). Examinees familiar with U.S. ADA standards confuse 1:12 (the ADA standard) with the Philippine preferred slope. In the Philippine context, 1:12 is a ceiling, not a target. Answering '1:12' for 'what is the standard slope' is wrong.
common_misconceptions: Importing U.S. ADA slope standards — ADA uses 1:12 as its standard; BP 344 uses 1:20 as preferred
Treating 1:20 and 1:12 as interchangeable — they are the preferred and maximum values respectively

questions.explanation: Critical: 1:20 = preferred; 1:15 = acceptable; 1:12 = maximum. The 'standard' is 1:20, not 1:12.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR App. A, Ramps; Trap #1

questions.text: According to Trap #40?, what are the two values that examinees frequently swap when describing the tactile warning strip specification — and which value is the depth versus the setback?

options.text: Depth = 300 mm; setback = 600 mm from the hazard edge — the strip is narrow and placed well back
Depth = 600 mm; setback = 300 mm from the hazard edge — the strip is wide and placed close to the hazard
Depth = 600 mm; setback = 600 mm from the hazard edge — both dimensions are equal for simplicity
Depth = 300 mm; setback = 300 mm from the hazard edge — both dimensions match for easy recall

rationale.summary: Trap #40: depth = 600 mm (the strip itself); setback = 300 mm (how far back from the hazard it is placed).
rationale.explanation: Trap #40 in the article describes this as the most-swapped pair of numbers in tactile specification. The tactile warning strip is 600 mm deep — meaning the strip occupies 600 mm of floor space measured perpendicular to the hazard. The near edge of the strip is placed 300 mm back from the hazard edge (stair nosing, ramp top, platform edge). The 300 mm setback ensures the user's foot detects the tactile warning before the leading foot reaches the drop. Selecting 300 mm as the depth is the documented wrong answer.
common_misconceptions: Selecting depth = 300 mm — 300 mm is the setback distance, not the strip depth
Treating both values as equivalent or interchangeable — they measure completely different things

questions.explanation: Tactile strip: 600 mm deep (the strip), 300 mm setback (from the hazard). Exam trap: these two numbers are frequently swapped.
